64: Sustainable transportation isn't just a technology swap. It's a Wicked Problem: economic pressures, environmental limits, technical constraints, social effects, and policy, all tangled together, and none of them can be solved in isolation. That tangle is why this research exists: transportation still drives a huge share of global CO2 emissions, and fossil-fuel alternatives need a real decision-making framework, not guesswork.
65: Running out of fossil carbon isn't the danger. Reserves are vast, and depletion is centuries away. The real emergency is atmospheric CO2, climbing every year, threatening life on this planet on a far shorter timeline.
68: Four thousand five hundred million years of natural optimisation, and nature never chose to store hydrogen. It splits water through photosynthesis, produces H2, and immediately locks it into biomolecules instead [1][8]. No stockpile. Global warming, meanwhile, is not a theory anymore. It's an empirical fact, backed by mountains of observational data [12]. The first climate prediction model appeared a century ago [13]. Sixteen years later, GS Callendar (1938) published the paper that tied climate change directly to human carbon dioxide output [14]. It took decades for that idea to reach public consciousness. And even now, despite behavioral shifts everyone agrees are desirable, over half of all anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions have happened in just the last 30 years. No reversal in sight.
69: The Treaties of Paris (1951) and Rome (1957) locked in institutional rules for coal and nuclear only. Oil, gas, renewables: each EU Member State was left to write its own national policy [20]. That changed. Europe became a driver of sustainability policy in its own right, and in March 2007 the European Council did something it had never done before: it agreed on an integrated climate and energy policy, complete with an Energy Action Plan for 2007-2009. The target that came out of it: 20% renewables in energy use by 2020 [21], [22].
72: Figure 1 shows a dimension people tend to skip over: time. Fossil fuels take 106-108 years to form geologically. We burn them in a fraction of that. That mismatch is the whole problem. Hitting climate targets means switching to low-carbon cycles (photosynthetic production, synthetic refining) that run on human timescales instead, somewhere around 10-2 to 10-5 years. And time matters just as much on the ground: refuelling, charging, logistics. A business runs on minutes, not geologic ages.
76: Figure 2 lays out the five criteria a viable alternative fuel has to clear: carbon neutrality for environmental stability, compatibility with existing engines, compatibility with existing infrastructure, a reliable feedstock supply, and financial viability. Miss one, and the fuel doesn't scale.
77: The European Parliament answered with the European Climate Law: climate neutrality by 2050, a minimum 55% cut in net greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 [4], [5]. But policy like this carries real social and economic weight. Take the EU's original plan to phase out internal combustion engines by 2035. It triggered serious pushback [6]. Former Stellantis CEO Carlos Tavares put it bluntly: mandating one specific technology, like EVs, without defining the broader goal, risks real social disruption and ignores the automotive industry's social dimension entirely [7].
78: The literature backs him up. Ignore affordability, employment, equity, and policy fails; inequality deepens [Pye et al. 2008; Mearns and Norton 2010].
79: This PhD program tries to close that gap. It pairs academic knowledge with a formal non-academic partnership, aimed squarely at the political and corporate decisions that shape people's lives. The candidate brings entrepreneurial and business management experience to the table, and the research leans on it: practical business problems first, so sustainability models stay tethered to operational reality instead of floating off into theory.
81: You have to understand demand before you can substitute fossil fuels. Transportation depends on them more than any other end-use sector [53]. And energy availability shifts by geography. Vehicles need fuel delivered directly, wherever they are. That single fact explains most of why fossil fuels are so stubborn to replace here.
82: EV adoption has picked up speed [57]. The barriers haven't gone anywhere, though: energy density, geographical variability, the infrastructure buildout, lifecycle emissions [58], battery supply chains [62]. Real, technical, and stacked against a fast transition.
85: Elsevier's 2021 report, "Pathways to Net Zero: The Impact of Clean Energy Research" [9], maps this complexity with data mining, and the visuals make the point well. Finding fossil fuel alternatives isn't a job for one discipline. It needs multidisciplinarity (co-authors crossing fields) and interdisciplinarity, real diversity of disciplines, not just adjacent specialists nodding at each other.
86: That complexity breeds a crisis of method. Publications keep multiplying, a Data Deluge, and a traditional Systematic Literature Review is obsolete before you finish writing it. Researchers get stuck with a false choice: narrow the scope and lose the systemic view fleet management actually needs, or drown. Decision-making needs both broad understanding and deep domain knowledge at once. Right now, it rarely gets either.
87: The crisis isn't just about volume. It's about vocabulary. The energy transition has outgrown the words we use to manage it. A fleet manager doesn't ask "which fuel?" anymore. The real question is "which way of putting range into a vehicle?" And there's no single word for the answer. "Fuel" excludes battery charging. "Energy carrier" names the vector, not the act of supplying a vehicle. This isn't a linguistics problem, either. It's operational. "Refuelling time" assumes a fuel exists. Infrastructure statistics count installed kilowatts when what a fleet operator actually needs is deliverable kilometres per stop. Even word embeddings, which cluster similar terms together, likely inherit the same blind spot, since they're trained on the very language that's missing the category in the first place. Section 2.1.1 develops this as a literature finding. Section 4.3 redefines replenishment metrics around it. And it sets up the first validation pilot for the Semantic Drift programme, Section 3.3.5.
89: This research treats AI as a systematic navigation tool for exactly that complexity. The topic was chosen before modern Generative AI even existed, back when sorting valuable information out of the daily flood of publications was already brutally hard.
90: Then Generative AI arrived, and it brought its own problems. Telling helpful information from "garbage" isn't easy when the tools generating it are opaque. Here's the paradox: endless data, powerful AI, and well-informed decisions are still just as hard to reach.
91: So this research looked at Retrieval-Augmented Generation and semantic similarity to get past what traditional SLRs can't do. The probabilistic approach did restructure knowledge systematically. It also brought risk with it: hallucinations, the "Stochastic Parrot" problem, where the AI says something plausible and wrong.
92: Here's the core argument: Generative AI's probabilistic nature isn't a flaw to work around. It's an opportunity, if you constrain it properly. Add deterministic validation layers, and AI can restructure enormous amounts of knowledge into something a human can actually handle. Probabilistic generation, paired with deterministic verification. That pairing is what builds reliable decision pathways.
94: Building a dynamic multi-criteria decision tool for transport systems means merging two very different data types: hard science grounded in chemistry and thermodynamics, and quantitative and qualitative input from stakeholders. This work takes a business-oriented route to that merge: knowledge transfer that bridges academic theory and high-TRL operational reality, with AI tools doing the heavy lifting.
95: One intuition kept surfacing throughout this research: AI's probabilistic nature doesn't automatically respect scientific epistemology. Leave a model to predict the next token statistically, with no structural constraints, and it drifts, away from what the user meant, sometimes away from the laws of physics entirely. This work has a name for that: Semantic Drift.
96: So within a Transport Systems doctoral program, bringing AI in isn't a detour from the real subject. It's a methodological answer to the field's own complexity, one built specifically to keep that drift in check.
97: Three constraints tie every artifact in this thesis together: time, location, and information, all under scarcity. Call it the scarcity triad. It governs fleet operations directly: vehicles, fuel, chargers, driver hours, all finite, all scattered unevenly across geography. It governs the research process too. The data deluge is really just cognitive capacity running scarce against publication volume, and AI-assisted synthesis runs under its own computational quota. Time binds twice over. Energy replenishment takes time. Decisions have deadlines. A perfect fuel choice delivered after the procurement window closes is worth nothing operationally. Every chapter that follows touches at least two of these three dimensions. Strip the framework down to its essence, and it's a method for making transport decisions reliably when all three constraints bind at once.
98: Main Objective: Develop and validate a dynamic, AI-enhanced knowledge structuring framework, one that safely turns multidisciplinary inputs into hard constraints, supporting operational Transport Systems decisions on fuel and energy-supply selection.
100: Map the complex transport ecosystem and its alternative fuels (methanol, hydrogen, electricity) through a systematic read of the extensive academic literature.
101: Identify operational and technology-specific constraints from that literature, using a structured data-extraction pipeline.
102: Formally define the neurosymbolic architecture behind the knowledge-structuring compiler, DSAiVE: a design that pairs a probabilistic language model with a rule-based mathematical validator, along with its deterministic validation layers.
103: Validate the framework through a high-TRL proof-of-concept: a 500-vehicle corporate fleet in Portugal, with literature-derived constraints folded directly into operational Vehicle Routing Problems and predictive maintenance.
105: This chapter works through the scientific literature on transportation energy systems and sustainability. Not just a survey of technological alternatives, though. The real goal is to diagnose what's structurally broken in how we synthesize knowledge and support decisions today. Two jobs, really. Consolidate what's already understood about alternative fuels and transport systems. And justify why the methodology needs to shift toward AI-assisted, epistemically constrained synthesis, a necessary condition, not an optional upgrade, for high-TRL operational decision-making.
106: Before an AI-driven "epistemic compiler" makes sense, the fundamental constraints of the transportation energy landscape need mapping first. What follows gets dense: chemical, thermodynamic, and logistical detail on alternative fuels, section by section. That density is deliberate. It's the "Technical Substrate": precise, multidimensional data, exactly the kind that overwhelms a traditional human-led literature review. Which is the point. It's the justification for the methodological shift this work makes later.
108: Technological maturity doesn't scale linearly into operational feasibility, not anywhere in the literature. Decision frameworks need to handle context-dependent, constraint-driven trade-offs. Universal rankings don't cut it.
110: Evaluating the shift away from fossil fuels starts with one distinction: primary energy sources versus energy carriers [28]. Electricity is a carrier. Zero mass, travels near light speed, brutal to store at scale, yet generated from all kinds of primary sources [29]. Get this distinction wrong, and any sustainability comparison collapses.
111: These options aren't a homogeneous class, and pretending otherwise causes problems. Diesel is the fossil incumbent. LPG plays transitional fuel. Methanol and dimethyl ether are candidate synthetics; their climate merit hinges entirely on renewable synthesis and where the carbon comes from. Ammonia and hydrogen get grouped together under the EU's Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, AFIR (Regulation (EU) 2023/1804), as alternative fuels for zero-emission transport, though their real climate performance still depends on production route. And battery-electric charging isn't a fuel at all, not in the conventional sense. That heterogeneity exposes a gap in the language itself, one with real operational consequences: there's no single category word left for what a vehicle takes on board. "Fuel" excludes charging. "Energy carrier" names the vector, one level removed from the actual act of supplying a vehicle. So this thesis adopts a working term instead, vehicle energy supply options, consistent with AFIR's deliberately broad statutory definition of "alternative fuels" in Article 2, point (4), which already includes electricity. This isn't pedantry. The absence of a common comparison unit at the "fuel" level is exactly what gave rise to the technology-agnostic Range Replenishment Capacity index in Section 4.3, the one place these options can actually be compared: delivered range per vehicle stop.
112: Electricity: EVs are the benchmark for decarbonization, sure. They're also stuck with real hurdles [68]. Battery technology still struggles with energy density, weight, cost; storage at scale is a genuine bottleneck [69]. Electrifying at any real scale demands massive infrastructure investment [70]. Renewables are intermittent, which complicates supply reliability and forces the need for robust storage just to keep the flow stable [73]. And then there's the battery supply chain itself: lifecycle emissions, extraction dependencies, the ethical weight of "extractivist" practices that comes with it [62].
113: Hydrogen: promising, but green hydrogen runs into economic limits fast; production is expensive [75]. Low volumetric energy density complicates storage and transport [76], meaning high-pressure or cryogenic tanks, both energy-hungry. It's highly flammable, so safety measures have to be strict [77]. And distribution infrastructure barely exists yet; building it out demands serious investment [78].
114: Methanol and Emerging Carriers: Methanol has real advantages: it fits existing liquid fuel infrastructure, and it can be produced from captured CO2 [79]. Production is energy-intensive, though [80], and toxicity plus a low boiling point make handling tricky [81]. Still, its emissions-reduction potential earns it a spot as a serious transition candidate [82], [83]. Other carriers follow the same pattern. Dimethyl Ether [84], [85], [87] and Ammonia [88], [89], [90] both burn clean and can ride established distribution networks, but energy density, engine modification needs, and toxicity limit them too.
116: Technological promises are easy to find. The fundamental sciences set the real bounds on what's feasible. Evaluating energy carriers properly means looking at three interconnected physical layers:
117: Classical Thermodynamics and Chemistry, the theoretical limits: energy can't be created or destroyed, only transformed. That's the first law [94]. The second law is less forgiving: irreversibility. No energy transformation hits 100% efficiency, ever; some is always lost as waste heat, and entropy climbs [95]. Physical chemistry adds the molecular detail: Gibbs Free Energy, for instance, predicts whether a reaction in a fuel cell or electrolysis process happens spontaneously at all [82], [96].
118: Exergy, the quality of energy: exergy analysis measures not how much energy exists, but how much useful work it can still do. Energy is conserved. Exergy isn't; it gets consumed. That makes it the right tool for finding exactly where transport systems waste potential [91], [97].
119: Finite-Time Thermodynamics, the temporal constraint: classical thermodynamics assumes infinite time to reach ultimate efficiency. Real transport systems don't get infinite time. They run on Finite-Time Thermodynamics instead. Tsirlin et al. (2025) make the case directly: optimising irreversible processes means accounting for how long the energy exchange actually takes. The goal stops being theoretical maximum efficiency. It becomes maximum power output, delivered within the time you actually have.
120: Time shows up explicitly in finite-time thermodynamics, in dynamic exergy formulations, and again in every study on charging, refuelling, queueing, infrastructure reliability. What's missing is the layer that ties it all together, the question nobody's fully answered: how much useful work can a transport system actually deliver, at what rate, with what waiting risk, at what reliability? This isn't "time versus exergy." It's the absence of operational exergy metrics that fold exergy, power, response time, queueing, and uptime into one transport-service framework.
121: That loss of fidelity, the temporal dimension especially, is exactly why synthesis mechanisms need to preserve physical limits as first-order inputs, not afterthoughts, in operational decision models.
123: Look at where energy supply meets demand, and transportation and location optimisation turn out to matter enormously. The frameworks historically used to evaluate this, though, usually miss the temporal and physical constraints laid out above.
125: Evaluating energy alternatives and their systemic impacts traditionally leans on a handful of established frameworks: Life Cycle Assessment [93], Techno-Economic Analysis [92]. For comparing fuels specifically, Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis earns its keep: economic, environmental, social, technical criteria, weighted and ranked [102]. Bibliometric analysis rounds it out, giving a wide-angle view of the academic knowledge base [9].
126: Useful, yes. But the literature keeps flagging the same structural cracks in these traditional frameworks:
127: Static Assumptions: predefined weights, fixed assumptions; most frameworks freeze the world in place and miss how operational reality actually evolves (Cinelli et al., 2014).
128: Boundary Sensitivity: move the system boundary an inch, and the results shift. They're notoriously sensitive to how the researcher frames the initial scenario (Finnveden et al., 2009).
129: Exclusion of Dynamics: time-of-day grid carbon intensity, real-time charging availability; dynamics like these get simplified away or dropped entirely (Beloin-Saint-Pierre et al., 2020).
130: Narrative Bias and Author Subjectivity: cross disciplines, and subjective narrative bias creeps into the synthesis. Authors' own disciplinary focus, funding sources both bias the claims that end up in the literature, usually toward overestimating a technology's viability and downplaying its operational drawbacks (Gough et al., 2012; Boutron & Ravaud, 2018).
131: Put those limitations together, and the conclusion is clear: traditional decision frameworks need an upstream data filter: something structured, that keeps relevant knowledge preserved, traceable, correctly mapped, before any numbers get aggregated.
133: Macro-level fuel evaluations shape global energy strategy. Fine. But the actual transition to sustainable transport happens at the micro-operational level, and that's where the literature needs to shift focus: toward Operations Research. The Vehicle Routing Problem sits at the center of this, along with its advanced variants. Heuristics and metaheuristics do the heavy lifting: Variable Neighbourhood Search, for instance, systematically varies a candidate solution's neighbourhood structure to escape local optima, which fits fleet routing problems with time windows, mixed vehicle types, and charging constraints particularly well. The goal throughout: minimize travel time and energy consumption (Hansen et al., 2019, demonstrate this on complex logistics networks).
134: IoT and vehicle telemetry brought something else with them: Predictive Maintenance, now a genuine strategic lever. Machine Learning predicting component failure doesn't just extend vehicle lifecycles; it cuts operational downtime dramatically (Carvalho et al., 2019). But nobody's tied these domains together. Dynamic routing, predictive maintenance, strategic vehicle substitution: the literature treats them as separate silos, not one interconnected operational ecosystem. That's a recognised, and still open, gap.
138: Transportation Systems research reaches well past infrastructure design. Social Sciences studies user behaviour. Mechanical Engineering handles vehicle power. Electrical Engineering covers charging grids. Computer Science builds the routing algorithms [111], [112], [113]. Environmental science weighs in too, on air quality and the sustainable mobility paradigm [114]. None of that fits inside one discipline. The field demands a genuinely interdisciplinary framework, full stop.
140: Knowledge production keeps accelerating, and that makes multidisciplinarity even more necessary. Scientific articles pile up exponentially. Digesting the knowledge base gets harder. Finding the publications actually relevant to a specific operational question gets harder too.
141: Table 1 puts numbers to that trend: recent publication growth across the key energy and transport domains, sourced from Scopus, 2023.
174: Look at "Green Methanol": over half of everything ever published on it came out in a single two-year window. Growth like that flips the bottleneck entirely. It's no longer information scarcity limiting research. It's selection and synthesis capacity. Screening that volume of publications for credibility, during an SLR, becomes brutally difficult. And that's when epistemic governance stops being a footnote and becomes the central research challenge.
176: Subject complexity plus a rising publication rate. That combination demands better tools. Traditionally, researchers reach for Rayyan [117] to organise articles, or bibliometric packages like Bibliometrix [118], [125]. Useful for macro-level insight. Fall apart, though, the moment you need something detailed, synthetic, or operational.
177: AI, specifically LLMs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation, promises real transformation here [122]. Early tests exposed the cracks fast, though. Models hit the "Lost in the Middle" problem: relevant information buried deep in a long text just gets skipped over, systematically [121]. Worse: LLMs drift semantically, hallucinate, generate statements that sound completely plausible and happen to be wrong [123]. Let probabilistic AI select and synthesize source data on its own, with no structural constraints, and you've introduced risk no engineering or policy decision at this scale can absorb.
179: The literature has gaps, and they're not small ones. The biggest: nothing connects primary energy sources to the operational reality of where they're actually consumed. Fueling a vehicle with liquid fuel takes five minutes. Charging a battery takes hours. That difference is enormous operationally, and traditional literature barely touches it.
180: That leaves a gap: vast, unstructured academic literature on one side, hard mathematical constraints for running a real transport fleet on the other. Closing it needs a new paradigm. The candidate's earlier work, "An AI Framework for Literature Review in Search of Sustainable Fuels" (Publication 2), makes the case directly: stop treating AI as a probabilistic oracle guessing at the State-of-the-Art. Use it instead as a knowledge-structuring compiler, something that pulls out verifiable atomic facts and puts them through strict, human-defined structural validation. Run this through the scarcity triad from Section 1.4 (time, location, information, all scarce) and the data-to-operations gap turns out to be a scarcity problem itself. Access to information isn't the binding constraint anymore. Time and cognitive capacity are, the resources needed to convert information into constraints tied to a specific place and moment. Data used to be scarce. Now decision time is.
182: This literature review stayed open and systemic in its early stages. Fair enough. But there's a reality of modern research that needs naming here. Researchers, at some point in their intellectual development, go looking for established authors who validate what they already believe. It's comforting. It's also confirmation bias: gathering evidence that fits the hypothesis, ignoring what contradicts it. Well documented, and not exactly a secret (Lipton & Steinhardt, 2019; Macoun & Miller, 2014).
183: Generative AI and "Deep Search" tools change that dynamic completely, though. Now a researcher can find validating claims and weave them into a plausible narrative at speeds nobody had before. Messeri and Crockett (2024), writing in Nature, call the result an "illusion of understanding": retrieval outpaces critical evaluation, and the gap between the two is where the illusion lives. LLMs add their own twist: sycophancy. They tailor retrieved evidence to whatever hypothesis the user seems to be implying (Perez et al., 2022). And it compounds. AI-assisted workflows can amplify Semantic Drift recursively, when one AI-generated framing feeds straight into the next AI's context with no human checkpoint in between; this project hit that exact failure mode itself (see Section 4.1, the 26 L/100km episode). So this thesis treats external validation (expert surveys, supervisor review, deterministic physical constraints) as mandatory. Not a nice-to-have. The grounding layer of the entire workflow, extending the bias argument from just the output to the whole process.
184: That means putting AI into the research workflow comes with a heavier responsibility attached. If it can validate any claim instantly, the researcher's job has to get harder, not easier: understanding exactly how a counter-argument could tear that claim down. The shift required: stop using AI to confirm. Start using it to falsify.
185: AI's speed needs a counterweight, rigorous and deterministic validation, and that realisation is what drives the methodology in the next chapter. Not a framework that just retrieves information. One that stress-tests it against competing operational constraints, actively. The question driving it: how do you build something that pulls verifiable constraints out of this literature and feeds them straight into fleet-level decision models?
